summary:
South Sulawesi stands under Indonesia's national framework, which is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. In Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025.

Physical risk is rising across Indonesia. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and reporting in August 2026 ties the surge to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism. Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue: on 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman, with Amnesty International stating the gathering violated no law and calling the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and no national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Within that framework South Sulawesi carries its own layer of proposed restriction. In April 2025 the Mayor of Makassar reaffirmed a commitment to pushing an anti-LGBT regional regulation (Perda) after a same-sex act at a night-entertainment venue went viral, and the deputy chair of the DPRD Makassar law-drafting body (Bapemperda) voiced support, arguing such a regulation is needed to preserve moral and religious norms. The episode marks a formal municipal push in Makassar toward an anti-LGBT regulation in 2025.

The push is not isolated. The OutRight Action International report 'Creeping Criminalisation' by Katjasungkana and Wieringa covers eight Indonesian provinces, South Sulawesi among them, and records how provincial and city bylaws criminalise same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity under regional autonomy. Sub-national instruments of this kind therefore already operate in the province alongside the national code.

As of April 2026 the Makassar rule remains proposed (Ranperda) rather than enacted. The Makassar city government's women's-empowerment and child-protection agency (DP3A) is intensifying LGBT 'prevention' through socialisation and education aimed at school-age children, plus case handling with counselling and a safe house for reported individuals, in response to community reports; DP3A head Ita Isdiana Anwar says most reports come from worried families. DPRD Kota Makassar member Muchlis Misbah, citing a Komisi D monitoring meeting that showed rising LGBT numbers alongside HIV/AIDS cases, backs the pending Ranperda on HIV/AIDS and LGBT as legal reinforcement.

The proposal has been in the legislative pipeline since at least January 2023, when Makassar's anti-LGBT raperda entered the 2023 local legislative programme (prolegda) as a 'priority for discussion'. Two DPRD Makassar members, including PKS-faction member Azwar ST, said the proposal models itself on Perda already passed elsewhere such as Bogor. Constitutional-law expert Bivitri Susanti called such raperdas a 'trend ahead of the political year' that risks worsening discrimination and persecution of LGBT people, and noted that the central government does little to stop discriminatory local regulations.
tangentialFactors:
South Sulawesi sits inside a documented national pattern rather than an exception: the 'Creeping Criminalisation' report identifies eight Indonesian provinces where provincial and city bylaws reach same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity, so a visitor moving between provinces encounters overlapping national and regional instruments rather than a single code.

The Makassar proposal is one of several such instruments cited as a model by local legislators; DPRD members pointed to Perda already passed in other cities, including Bogor, when arguing for adoption. Constitutional-law expert Bivitri Susanti characterised the spread of these raperdas as a trend ahead of a political year and warned it risks worsening discrimination and persecution of LGBT people.

The central government's posture matters to the trajectory: Susanti noted that Jakarta does little to stop discriminatory local regulations, which leaves sub-national restriction largely unchecked by national review.

Local framing links LGBT regulation to public health, with a DPRD Makassar member citing a Komisi D monitoring meeting that reported rising LGBT numbers alongside HIV/AIDS cases. That association raises the likelihood that the pending instrument is presented as health enforcement rather than purely moral legislation.

At national level the direction of travel is toward harder enforcement: a presidential decree of October 2025 places LGBTQ+ people inside national defence policy as a non-military threat, and reporting in August 2026 ties that framing to a rise in vigilante attacks on transgender people.
localsOnly:
Residents of Makassar live under an active municipal prevention apparatus. The city government's women's-empowerment and child-protection agency (DP3A) runs socialisation and education aimed at school-age children, case handling with counselling, and a safe house for individuals reported to the agency; DP3A head Ita Isdiana Anwar says most reports come from worried families. The reporting channel therefore runs through households rather than through complaints by the person concerned.

The legislative route for the local rule runs through the DPRD Makassar and its law-drafting body, Bapemperda. The proposal entered the 2023 local legislative programme as a priority for discussion, drew mayoral reaffirmation in April 2025, and remained a Ranperda rather than an enacted Perda as of April 2026, with DPRD member Muchlis Misbah pressing for it as legal reinforcement alongside a pending Ranperda on HIV/AIDS.

Residents also remain subject to the national layer: the penal code in force since 2 January 2026, the 2006 pornography statute, and the absence of any national non-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the Makassar Ranperda on HIV/AIDS and LGBT has been enacted after April 2026. The most recent sourced status is that it remained proposed as of that date; no later legislative record is available here.

Unresolved: whether other cities or districts in South Sulawesi have enacted their own anti-LGBT bylaws. The 'Creeping Criminalisation' report covers South Sulawesi among eight provinces, but the specific instruments in force elsewhere in this province are not itemised in the available sources.

Not sourced: any record of enforcement under a South Sulawesi regional regulation, since none is confirmed enacted, and any documented instance of a foreign visitor being prosecuted under a Makassar instrument.

Unresolved: how the national penal code provisions in force since 2 January 2026 have been applied in South Sulawesi specifically. National reporting describes prosecutions as selective rather than systematic but does not break down provincial case data.

Not sourced: whether DP3A's counselling and safe-house referrals are voluntary, and what legal basis or oversight governs them.
